2:260.en: And when Abraham said (unto his Lord): My Lord! Show me how Thou givest life to the dead, He said: Dost thou not believe? Abraham said: Yea, but (I ask) in order that my heart may be at ease. (His Lord) said: Take four of the birds and cause them to incline unto thee, then place a part of them on each hill, then call them, they will come to thee in haste, and know that Allah is Mighty, Wise

shksM8YdDfg.speaker: adnan
shksM8YdDfg.speaker_note: 15th installment of his 'Achieving the Balance' series
shksM8YdDfg.title: Achieving the Balance: Between Understanding the Wisdom and Full Submission
shksM8YdDfg.one_line: Everything Allah creates and commands has wisdom, but faith cannot depend on explaining everything; a Muslim submits, then serves those who suffer.
shksM8YdDfg.summary: The fifteenth balance khutbah opens with the undisputed part: Allah created nothing aimlessly, the cosmos serves a purpose, and every command ends with its aim, such as taqwa or guidance. The balance is that knowing there is wisdom does not mean you will always see it. Faith built on needing an explanation for every event will eventually collapse, because the word Muslim means one who submits unconditionally. He argues that believers trust Allah because of pain, not despite it: at the Trench the believers saw ten thousand enemies and said this is what Allah promised, and the Quran states that trials are promised to every claimant of faith. Those who understand do not ask why disasters happen; they get up and relieve suffering. No one knows why the people of Yunus were spared and Pharaoh was not. Ibrahim, the most questioning prophet, who reasoned about idols and stars and asked to see resurrection, submitted when told to sacrifice his son without any reason given. Applying this to the recent earthquake and to a toddler dying of cancer, he says servants provide the service and do not question the Master, and he condemns those who explain catastrophes as punishment for victims' sins as arrogant and harmful.

outline.heading: Opening
Nothing was created for play
outline.gist: Undisputed ground: everything Allah created has a purpose and every command has a goal. Did you think We created you aimlessly and that you would not return to Us?

outline.heading: Creation subjected to serve you
outline.gist: Rain, ships, rivers, sun, moon, night and day are placed at your disposal; the sun and moon let you count your years; the oaths by winds and clouds show that everything has a role.

outline.heading: Every command ends with its aim
outline.gist: Verses on prayer, fasting and zakah close with their goal: taqwa, guidance, the straight path. Beyond the truth there is only error, and he recites further verses on purposeful creation.

outline.heading: Wisdom you will not always see
outline.gist: Knowing there is wisdom behind everything does not mean you will know it. Faith built on needing an explanation for every event will, with certainty, be lost.

outline.heading: What 'Muslim' means
outline.gist: A Muslim is one who accepts unconditionally what Allah says and does, including what cannot be explained.

outline.heading: Because of the pain, not despite it
outline.gist: Atheists reject God because of suffering and some Muslims believe despite it; he argues believers trust Allah because of it, since He foretold it.

outline.heading: The Trench: this is what Allah promised
outline.gist: After ten days of digging, the believers saw ten thousand Confederates and said this is what Allah promised, while the doubters called the promise a lie; the sight only strengthened their faith.

outline.heading: Trials are promised to every claimant of faith
outline.gist: We do not question Allah; we respond. People will not be left to say 'we believe' without being tested, so Allah makes evident who is truthful and who strives and perseveres.

outline.heading: Shaken until they asked when help would come
outline.gist: Earlier believers were shaken to their core until the Prophet and those with him asked when Allah's help would come; it is near. The question is what you do when trials come.

outline.heading: We have exaggerated our power to explain
outline.gist: Having worked out the reasons for some commands, people think everything must be explainable and lose faith when something is not. A Muslim accepts what Allah decreed either way.

outline.heading: Put your head down and do the job
outline.gist: When catastrophe strikes, the ignorant ask why and who; those who understand go and relieve the suffering. Questioning Allah is beyond your and my payroll.

outline.heading: Why were the people of Yunus spared?
outline.gist: Yunus's people were warned of punishment and then spared, while Pharaoh was not. We do not know why, never will, and it is not our business.

outline.heading: Ibrahim told to sacrifice his son
outline.gist: He is not preaching blind faith and has been criticized for saying the opposite, but no one can give a reason for slaughtering an only son; the Quran praises the moment they both submitted.

outline.heading: Ibrahim the questioner: idols and stars
outline.gist: Ibrahim is the most intellectual prophet in the Quran: he broke the idols to expose them and reasoned through the star, moon and sun.

outline.heading: Shown the birds, yet submitting without a reason
outline.gist: He asked to see how Allah revives the dead and was shown the birds on the mountains, yet when no reason for the sacrifice could be found he submitted, which is what Muslim means.

outline.heading: A child's cancer: servants serve, not question
outline.gist: Some things, like a toddler dying of cancer, have no explanation available to us. His job is to submit, comfort and help the family; servants provide the service and do not question the Master, and one day Allah will explain.

outline.heading: The earthquake and the arrogance of blaming victims
outline.gist: Forcing an explanation on the earthquake leads people to say the victims were punished for their sins. That is arrogance and speaking without knowledge, and it drives people from faith; we ask for mercy, help and thank Allah we were spared.

outline.heading: Outro

rtA8Kn0h7p0.speaker: adnan
rtA8Kn0h7p0.speaker_note: regular Sunday tafseer series, single speaker; refers to his own patients and his teacher
rtA8Kn0h7p0.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Waqi'ah, Part 5 (56:75-96)
rtA8Kn0h7p0.one_line: The oath by the positions of the stars, the nobility of the Quran, the soul at the throat, and the three final destinations.
rtA8Kn0h7p0.summary: He closes Al-Waqi'ah by recalling how the cluster of surahs from Qaf onward offers choices, ending with the three groups on the Day of Judgment, where worldly labels like degrees and nationality vanish. A one-in-three chance of ruin is not a gamble worth taking, and he describes the private reckoning, counting life as roughly four thousand weeks, and the verdict as the climax every life story should build toward. He then explains Allah's emphatic oath by the positions of the stars, linking nujum to the Quran revealed in instalments, the vastness of the cosmos and our smallness, and the three senses of karim: noble, rare and endlessly generous. The Quran is preserved and sent by the Lord of all that is not God. He asks why anyone would bargain away parts of this way of life or make denial their thanks for it, then describes the soul at the throat with Allah nearer than the family, citing the long hadith on death. He urges aiming to be among those brought near, removing the idea of deserving, and explains the levels of certainty. Finally he asks students to read the Quran as if it were revealed to them personally and to respond to Allah's communication.

outline.heading: Opening
Recap: the cluster of surahs as a series of choices
outline.gist: From Qaf onward each surah offers a choice: righteousness, purpose, guidance, certainty of knowledge, gratitude.

outline.heading: Three groups, and worldly labels dissolve
outline.gist: On the Day of Judgment degrees, professions and nationalities mean nothing; only how you lived decides your group.

outline.heading: A one-in-three risk is not worth gambling
outline.gist: Drawing on giving survival odds to patients, he argues no chance of ending in the wrong group is acceptable.

outline.heading: The private reckoning with your book
outline.gist: Narrations describe being brought before Allah, screened from others, and asked to read through your record.

outline.heading: A life is about four thousand weeks
outline.gist: A lifetime is about a thousand months; each week is like one page you must explain.

outline.heading: Asked also about what you did not do
outline.gist: You will be asked about the person Allah sent your way whom you brushed off because you were busy.

outline.heading: The verdict as the climax of your story
outline.gist: Hearing that you made it makes every hardship worthwhile; a life indifferent to that moment is like a film whose hero ignores the plot.

outline.heading: Those promised Paradise still feared
outline.gist: Companions who heard directly that they were in Jannah never lowered their guard; aim high.

outline.heading: Recitation note: prolongation counts in Hafs
outline.gist: Most prolongations are four counts in Hafs; a few places take six, which he points out.

outline.heading: An oath that begins 'No, I swear'
outline.gist: The la before the oath emphasises rather than negates: Allah does not need to swear but does so to stress what follows.

outline.heading: Nujum: the stars and the Quran revealed in instalments
outline.gist: The word evokes both stars in the sky and the Quran sent down in parts; the answer to the oath is that this is a noble Quran.

outline.heading: Karim: noble, rare and endlessly generous
outline.gist: The Quran is of high status, has nothing like it, and keeps giving the more you read it.

outline.heading: A mighty oath, if you only knew
outline.gist: Light years and galaxies are beyond comprehension; we are small and simple, yet were given this book.

outline.heading: In a protected record, touched only by the purified
outline.gist: The Quran is kept with Allah and handled only by the angels who carry it to the prophets.

outline.heading: We used to look up at the sky
outline.gist: Before phones people stared upward; most named stars carry Arabic names; the fiqh of touching the mushaf is not the point here.

outline.heading: Sent down by the Lord of all worlds
outline.gist: Al-'alamin is everything other than Allah, so unlike earlier scriptures sent to particular peoples, the Quran addresses all creation.

outline.heading: What else do you need to hear?
outline.gist: After such an oath, he asks what is still missing before one turns one's life around.

outline.heading: Hadith as a way of life
outline.gist: The word means a way of life and conduct, which is why the Prophet's sayings, actions and approvals are all called hadith.

outline.heading: Selling out on parts of the book
outline.gist: Mudhinun are those who compromise principles for gain; believers cannot bargain pieces of the deen away as people with nothing to lose do.

outline.heading: Making denial your thanks for provision
outline.gist: The Quran is the most elite provision; repaying it with denial and neglect is the ingratitude the verse condemns.

outline.heading: The soul at the throat, and We are nearer
outline.gist: As the family watches the dying, Allah and the angels of death are closer to the person than they are.

outline.heading: The long hadith of death and the grave
outline.gist: The Prophet sat by a grave, told them to seek refuge from its punishment, and described angels of light coming for the believer's soul.

outline.heading: If you are not accountable, hold the soul back
outline.gist: Madinin means held to account; no technology or ICU can keep the soul in, since every organ carries an expiry date.

outline.heading: If he is among those brought near
outline.gist: Those brought near are the forerunners from the start of the surah; aim to be among them.

outline.heading: Remove 'deserve' from your vocabulary
outline.gist: No one deserves anything from Allah, so feeling unworthy is no reason not to aim high.

outline.heading: Rest, fragrance and a garden of bliss
outline.gist: Rawh is a breath of relief that removes anxiety and emptiness; the highest reward is inner peace before anything physical.

outline.heading: Peace from the people of the right
outline.gist: They send their greetings of peace because they are doing well; there is no need to worry about them.

outline.heading: The deniers and the astray
outline.gist: Whether one rejects truth knowingly or drifts in indifference, the end is boiling water and burning fire.

outline.heading: The truth of certainty
outline.gist: He distinguishes certainty from knowledge, from seeing and from experience; on the Day you will experience it, so choose now which of the three you want.

outline.heading: Exalt the name of your Lord, the Most Great
outline.gist: The second time the command appears; glorify Allah and look inward for answers rather than blaming Him.

outline.heading: The closing passage drawn together
outline.gist: He retells the whole sequence from the oath to the three destinations in one sweep.

outline.heading: Interlude
Muslims missing the beauty of their book
outline.gist: It pains him that many Muslims only know the Quran from school or prayer and miss its depth and philosophy.

outline.heading: Three dimensions of the Quran
outline.gist: When a surah was revealed, where it sits in the mushaf, and what it does to you; only the third he cannot do for you.

outline.heading: Read it as if revealed to you
outline.gist: His teacher had students read as if they were the Prophet receiving it, then as if it were sent to them personally to practise and spread.

outline.heading: Allah's message awaits your response
outline.gist: Communication is two-way; Allah's side is done, and what remains is how you live by, defend and spread it.

outline.heading: Outro
Read the surah yourself first
outline.gist: Come to your own understanding before each lesson and compare, to build the skill of personal reflection.

outline.heading: Outro

e0FT0-DBM0A.speaker: adnan
e0FT0-DBM0A.speaker_note: regular Sunday tafseer series, single speaker throughout
e0FT0-DBM0A.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Waqi'ah, Part 4 (56:57-74)
e0FT0-DBM0A.one_line: Four questions in Al-Waqi'ah (procreation, crops, rain, fire) that strip away human arrogance and build full conviction that Allah created us.
e0FT0-DBM0A.summary: He presents this page of Al-Waqi'ah as the surah's philosophical case for choosing to be among the foremost or the people of the right. It opens with the challenge that Allah created us, so why do we not believe. He argues that when Muslims fail to practise, the root is often not weak will but a hidden doubt in conviction, and that untreated doubt spreads like a cancer. The passage then asks four questions about things everyone takes for granted. Who turns the fluid into a human being? Who makes the seed grow? Who sends fresh water from the clouds instead of salt? Who made the tree that gives fire? In each case our contribution is only to bring things together and hope. He uses embryology, fertility treatment, farming, the water cycle and the difficulty of even defining fire to show that science explains how a process works, never who set it in motion, and that understanding a process should deepen awe rather than replace God. Because religion rests on such simple shared facts, everyone can be held accountable. He closes with the command to exalt the name of the Lord and urges the audience to reach certainty, since certainty changes habits, behaviour and how one sees the world.

outline.heading: Al-Waqi'ah as a surah of choices
outline.gist: The surah keeps offering the listener a choice of who to be: guided or aimless, grateful or ungrateful.

outline.heading: A page that argues why you should choose well
outline.gist: Before the closing comparison, this page breaks off to give philosophical reasons to join the first two groups.

outline.heading: We created you, so why do you not believe?
outline.gist: The anchor verse: the proper response to being created is belief, and refusing it points to something unresolved inside.

outline.heading: Weak practice hides a problem of conviction
outline.gist: Beneath laziness and desire lies doubt; Makkan surahs focus on belief because once certainty is built, practice follows and no one can stop you.

outline.heading: Untreated doubt grows like cancer
outline.gist: Doubt never sits quietly; it spreads and eats the good around it unless dealt with.

outline.heading: Questions that force an answer
outline.gist: Like the repeated question in Ar-Rahman, these verses pose four questions about four basic things everyone agrees on.

outline.heading: The fluid you emit: do you create it?
outline.gist: Our role in procreation is only bringing two fluids together; the differentiation of cells into a human being is entirely beyond us.

outline.heading: Science explains how, not who
outline.gist: Science gives a more detailed description, not an answer to origin; confusing science with philosophy is a modern fallacy.

outline.heading: If the process simply stopped
outline.gist: If gametes stopped combining, no one could negotiate with them and humanity would vanish in a generation.

outline.heading: We decreed death and none can outrun Us
outline.gist: Every human carries an expiry date; Allah alone decrees the moment of death.

outline.heading: Replacing you and re-forming you in what you do not know
outline.gist: Our consciousness could have been channelled into any other form; being a functioning human is a gift we underrate.

outline.heading: Fertility clinics only make a better introduction
outline.gist: Even assisted reproduction just brings egg and sperm together; the intricate dance of DNA happens on its own.

outline.heading: You know the first creation, so why deny the second?
outline.gist: The same power that brought us out the first time can bring us out again; tadhakkur means reflecting on this.

outline.heading: Human arrogance after a little knowledge
outline.gist: Humans understand one equation and then deny God, because knowledge feels powerful; imagine the One who knows all.

outline.heading: The crops you sow: do you make them grow?
outline.gist: Zar' is making a seed become a plant that bears food; we supply soil, water and light, but a dead seed coming to life is not our doing.

outline.heading: Skilled farming versus the source of life
outline.gist: Farming expertise clutters the question with irrelevant detail; where the life in the plant comes from is untouched by it.

outline.heading: Turned to debris: we are ruined, we are deprived
outline.gist: If seeds stopped growing, people would wander speaking aimlessly in the language of doom, deprived of all food.

outline.heading: The water you drink: who sends it from the clouds?
outline.gist: All earth's water was salty; fresh reservoirs come from billions of years of the sun evaporating sea water at just the right distance.

outline.heading: Had We willed, We would have made it salty
outline.gist: Imagine acid or salt rain; we expect children, harvests and rain as givens and owe gratitude because we control none of it.

outline.heading: Ten years without rain
outline.gist: A region his family knew for deep snow turned near-desert after a decade of drought; people in water-rich places complain about rain because they have not seen its absence.

outline.heading: The fire you kindle and the tree that feeds it
outline.gist: We only create friction; Allah made the wood that burns, and human history changed once fire was harnessed.

outline.heading: A reminder and provision for travellers, and a thing we cannot define
outline.gist: Fire recalls punishment and serves those on life's journey; scientists still do not agree on what fire actually is.

outline.heading: Understanding the process should increase awe
outline.gist: Like a child who appreciates parents only once raising children, knowing how something works should deepen appreciation of who made it.

outline.heading: Simple basics everyone can be held to
outline.gist: Recap of the four questions; religion rests on facts all share equally, which is why everyone can be held accountable.

outline.heading: Exalt the name of your Lord, the Most Great
outline.gist: The closing command follows from the four questions: glorify the One who made it so.

outline.heading: Certainty changes how you live
outline.gist: Once this is not a probability but a certainty, it changes habits, behaviour and how one sees the world.

57:20.ar: ٱعۡلَمُوٓاْ أَنَّمَا ٱلۡحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنۡيَا لَعِبࣱ وَلَهۡوࣱ وَزِينَةࣱ وَتَفَاخُرُۢ بَيۡنَكُمۡ وَتَكَاثُرࣱ فِي ٱلۡأَمۡوَٰلِ وَٱلۡأَوۡلَٰدِۖ كَمَثَلِ غَيۡثٍ أَعۡجَبَ ٱلۡكُفَّارَ نَبَاتُهُۥ ثُمَّ يَهِيجُ فَتَرَىٰهُ مُصۡفَرࣰّ ا ثُمَّ يَكُونُ حُطَٰمࣰ اۖ وَفِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ عَذَابࣱ شَدِيدࣱ وَمَغۡفِرَةࣱ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرِضۡوَٰنࣱۚ وَمَا ٱلۡحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنۡيَآ إِلَّا مَتَٰعُ ٱلۡغُرُورِ

QhS2ayBIxcc.speaker: adnan
QhS2ayBIxcc.speaker_note: 14th in his 'Achieving the Balance' series, asks his congregation to close gaps
QhS2ayBIxcc.title: Achieving the Balance: Desire and Fear, and the High Point of Love
QhS2ayBIxcc.one_line: Muslims fly to Allah on two wings, desire for Paradise and fear of just punishment, which together should grow into love of Allah.
QhS2ayBIxcc.summary: Opening with Allah's command to tell His servants He is most forgiving and that His punishment is painful, the fourteenth balance khutbah takes the classical image of two wings: hope in Allah's reward and fear of His punishment. He starts with desire because he thinks his society needs it: nearly every long surah describes Paradise, and wanting it is an obligation. The companions lived for it: a man threw away his dates before battle, Haritha's mother was told her son was in the highest garden, and a lame companion insisted on fighting so he could walk into Paradise on his disabled leg. In the second khutbah he objects that fear of Hell has been watered down, though the Quran never mentions one without the other. He gives five points: concepts are only understood through their opposites, as entitled children show; fear is a strong short-term brake against sin; we fear not that Allah will oppress us but that He will judge us by pure justice instead of generosity; some truly deserve punishment, so make sure you are not among them; and life contains pain, so do not shield children from it. The pinnacle is love of Allah, which outlasts both and accepts whatever He wills.

outline.heading: Opening
Tell My servants: forgiving, and painful punishment
outline.gist: The khutbah rests on the verses in which Allah tells His servants that He is the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that His punishment is painful.

outline.heading: Two wings: desire and reverent fear
outline.gist: In the fourteenth balance khutbah he gives a thousand-year-old image: you fly to Allah with hope in His reward and reverent fear of His punishment; lose one wing and you fall.

outline.heading: Desire first: Paradise in nearly every surah
outline.gist: He starts with desire because this society needs it most. Every surah of a page or more describes what awaits, and he recites the promise of Paradise to those who stay the course.

outline.heading: Bliss on every level, and wanting it is a duty
outline.gist: Paradise holds pleasures for parts of the self we have not yet discovered. Wanting it is not wrong selfishness but an obligation to work toward.

outline.heading: The companion who threw away his dates
outline.gist: Told what awaits the one who stands his ground, a companion decided eating his dates was too long a wait, gave them away, fought and was martyred.

outline.heading: Haritha in the highest garden
outline.gist: A young man killed by an arrow before the battle began; his frightened mother demanded to know his fate and was told he is in the highest of the gardens.

outline.heading: The lame companion who would walk into Paradise
outline.gist: Told all his life he could not, he refused to stay home at Uhud so his disabled leg could march into Paradise. The Prophet let him go, and he ran his uneven run to defend the mountain until he fell.

outline.heading: They lived for it, and so must we
outline.gist: The companions gave everything to be among the people of Paradise; living with that desire is what every believer is required to do.

outline.heading: Interlude
Fear of punishment has been watered down
outline.gist: People avoid talk of punishment, yet the Quran never speaks of Paradise without Hell. The Prophet saw both and said that if you knew what he knew you would laugh little and weep much.

outline.heading: Point one: nothing is understood without its opposite
outline.gist: The mind defines things only by contrast: life means something only because of death, and reward only because of punishment.

outline.heading: The entitled child: reward needs its opposite
outline.gist: Parents who made sure their children never went without are frustrated that the children do not appreciate anything; they cannot, because they never knew lack. Paradise likewise needs Hell to be understood.

outline.heading: Point two: fear as a short-term brake
outline.gist: Fear is a poor long-term motive but a strong one at the moment of sin. Without consequences people eventually do anything; the thought of punishment makes you hold back from the forbidden.

outline.heading: Point three: we fear Allah's justice, not oppression
outline.gist: We fear that people will wrong us; we never fear that from Allah. We fear that He will treat us with only justice, when what we need is generosity far beyond what we deserve.

outline.heading: Two kinds of fear a child has of a father
outline.gist: A child can fear being mistreated or fear being treated fairly and not forgiven; our fear of Allah is the second kind. He recites verses from Al-Hadid on punishment.

outline.heading: Point four: some deserve punishment; do not be among them
outline.gist: Those who oppress, kill and strip others of rights beyond repair show why Hell exists. Your only concern is to make sure your choices do not place you among them.

outline.heading: The guilty would ransom everyone
outline.gist: On seeing Hell, the guilty wish to offer their children, spouses, brothers, clans and everyone on earth to escape it; whatever they saw must be terrible to provoke that.

outline.heading: Point five: life has pain; do not shield your children
outline.gist: Suffering is part of existence. Being a good Muslim means dealing with it well, so shielding children and people from pain and from the idea of punishment is unhealthy.

outline.heading: The pinnacle: love beyond desire and fear
outline.gist: Desire and fear are the starting wings; the high point is the love of Allah they generate in the heart, for the One who loved you long before you loved Him.

outline.heading: Love accepts whatever He wills
outline.gist: Once you love Him you accept whatever He gives or withholds, because what He wants for you is what you want. Love is the strongest and longest-lasting motive.

outline.heading: Outro

quran.point: Tell My servants I am the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that My punishment is painful: the two wings.
Paradise promised to those who stay the course, recited as a sample of what Allah has prepared.
Verses from Al-Hadid on punishment, recited as what the believer fears.
The guilty would ransom children, spouse, brother, clan and everyone on earth to escape Hell.

hadith.gist: Haritha's mother asked whether her son, killed by a stray arrow, was in Paradise; the Prophet said he is in the highest of the gardens.
If you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much.

maxims: We fly to Allah with two wings
Nowhere does the Quran mention Paradise without Hell
Fear is a good short-term motive, not long-term
We don't fear Allah's oppression; we fear His justice
Don't shield your children from pain

stories.who: A companion with dates before battle
stories.point: He threw away his dates rather than delay reaching Paradise, then fought until martyred.
Killed before the battle began, he reached the highest garden: Paradise was what the companions lived for.

stories.who: The lame companion at Uhud (Amr ibn al-Jamuh)
stories.point: Told all his life he could not, he insisted on fighting so his disabled leg could walk into Paradise; the Prophet let him go.

contemporary: Trend of downplaying Hell and punishment in current Islamic teaching
takeaways: Keep both hope in Allah's reward and fear of His punishment in your worship
Use fear as a brake at the moment of temptation
Make sure your choices, especially toward others, do not place you among those who deserve punishment
Do not shield your children from life's pain; teach them to handle it
Aim beyond hope and fear to love of Allah, accepting whatever He wills
